newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK MONEY MKT SQUEEZE MAY BOOST SHARES-DEALERS.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK MONEY MKT SQUEEZE MAY BOOST SHARES-DEALERS.

text.p: A liquidity squeeze on the Slovak interbank market has led to a lull in share trading but brokers say the equities market could revive as companies mull share offerings as a cheaper way to raise funds.

The Bratislava Stock Exchange (BSE), one of central Europe's smaller bourses with market capitalisation of $2.5 billion, was inundated with foreign buying earlier this year, sending the SAX index to fresh highs on an almost daily baisis.
But investment ebbed in May, mainly driven by enormously high interest rates on the money market making it expensive to raise the funds to buy shares. Thus, the BSE has been illiquid.
"I don't see any chance of a significant improvement, at least until the central bank would change its policy," Peter Krutil, chief trader at Creditanstalt Securities, told Reuters.

However, Krutil said that the current shortage of capital among some Slovak companies caused by high interest rates may parodixically offer a way out by itself, forcing cash-strapped firms to consider share offerings as an alternative to loans.
Overnight Slovak interbank rates were quoted at over 50 percent on Wednesday.

"This may force them to enter the capital market relatively soon," Krutil said. "I think investors would welcome any new reasonable share issues, as that is what this market has been desperately needing for years."
But, he added, a market revival driven by share offerings would not happen immediately because of the time involved in preparing the measure.

The thin market moved lower again on Wednesday. The SAX index eased 0.24 points to 190.49 in sluggish trading on Wednesday, with only 675 shares trading on the BSE's main floor, with turnover at just 572,440 crowns.
"The cruel policy of the National Bank of Slovakia has caused a slowing down of the growth of economy, with no money in the system," said Vladimir Kuklis, an analyst at Ceskoslovenska Obchodni Banka.

The Slovak money market has been suffering from a severe liquidity crunch, with the central bank (NBS) remaining vigiliant in its strategy of keeping the local money market short to prevent speculative attacks on the crown.
As of June 2, banks lacked around 15 billion crowns, or some 34.71 percent of the funds needed to meet its minimum reserve requirements later this month.
The free-flow of share capital traded on the BSE totals only $900 million, against some $5.0 billion on the Prague bourse, $4.6 billion in Warsaw and $3.5 billion in Budapest.
